nameStory: The Dotterel Filefish gets its curious name from the dotterel, a small shorebird known for being easily caught due to its trusting nature. Like its namesake bird, this filefish is considered somewhat simple or "dotty" in its behavior. The "filefish" part comes from their rough, sandpaper-like skin that feels like a metal file when rubbed the wrong way.
description: The Dotterel Filefish is a diamond-shaped fish with rough, sandpaper-textured skin that belongs to the filefish family. These unusual-looking fish have a compressed, oval body and can grow up to 18 inches long, though most are around 10-12 inches. They're peaceful plant-eaters that spend their time grazing on algae and seagrass in shallow coastal waters. With only two recorded sightings in New England, they're extremely rare visitors from warmer southern waters.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly compressed and diamond-shaped when viewed from the side, with a deep body that tapers to a narrow tail base

idTips.label: Skin Texture
idTips.description: Rough, sandpaper-like skin that feels coarse when rubbed backward - much rougher than typical fish scales

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single prominent dorsal spine on top of head, with soft dorsal and anal fins positioned far back near the small, fan-shaped tail

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small terminal mouth with protruding lips, positioned at the front tip of the pointed snout

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized fish reaching up to 18 inches, with most individuals measuring 10-12 inches in length

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found over seagrass beds, sandy, or muddy bottoms in shallow coastal waters, typically 30-300 feet deep

habitat: In New England's rare encounters, Dotterel Filefish would be found in shallow coastal waters over seagrass beds or sandy bottoms. They prefer areas with good algae growth and marine vegetation, typically in depths of 30-300 feet. These warm-water fish are occasional visitors that likely arrive during warmer months when Gulf Stream currents bring tropical species northward.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare, but any sightings would likely occur as waters begin warming and southern currents strengthen.
seasonality.summer: Most likely season for rare appearances when water temperatures peak and tropical species may drift north with warm currents.
seasonality.fall: Possible but less likely as waters begin cooling, though some tropical visitors may linger into early fall.
seasonality.winter: Virtually impossible to encounter as cold New England waters would be unsuitable for this warm-water species.

funFact: Dotterel Filefish are essentially underwater vegetarians - they're one of the few marine fish that are almost entirely herbivorous, spending their days peacefully munching on seagrass and algae like underwater cows grazing in a meadow!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with its relatives the Orange Filefish or Scrawled Filefish, but the Dotterel Filefish lacks the bright orange coloration of the former and the distinctive blue scrawled markings of the latter. Remember: if it's plain-colored with rough skin and diamond-shaped, think Dotterel.
contextualKnowledge: With only two recorded observations in New England, seeing a Dotterel Filefish here would be like spotting a tropical bird during a New England winter - possible but extraordinarily rare. These are primarily warm-water Atlantic fish that occasionally venture north, making any New England sighting noteworthy for marine biologists.
compareHints: Unlike its Orange Filefish relative which has bright orange coloration, or the Scrawled Filefish with its distinctive blue scribbly markings, the Dotterel Filefish is relatively plain in coloration. All three share the characteristic rough, file-like skin and compressed body shape, but the Dotterel Filefish is the most subdued in appearance. It's also typically smaller than the Scrawled Filefish, which can reach over 3 feet in length.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Orange filefish can be distinguished from its relatives, the dotterel filefish and scrawled filefish, by its solid orange coloration and smaller size.
Scrawled filefish are much larger and more distinctively patterned than their cousin the orange filefish, which is smaller and lacks the characteristic blue scribbles.
